Welcome toA Released String

A long string is held in one pulse and let go from rest: what does the pulse do?

About: d'Alembert's solution: a string released from rest divides into two half-height copies of its shape travelling apart at v

About this simulation

On screen
Top: the string u(x, t) as a solid blue curve over a dotted baseline, x from −50 to 50 cm, u from −0.5 to 2.5 mm (magnified). Once a run has reached 20 ms with the current shape, the right-going part ½u₀(x − vt) is dashed orange and the left-going part ½u₀(x + vt) dashed purple. Below: a map of u over x and t, painted up to the latest time reached, white at 0 and dark blue at 2.0 mm, with a thin line at the current time.
Controls
Initial pulse shape: smooth hump, triangle or rectangle, all 2.0 mm high with half-width 5.0 cm; changing it puts t back to 0, pauses, hides the dashed parts and clears the map. Time t: drag from 0 to 20 ms in steps of 0.25 ms, or type a time in the box beside the label (it rounds to the nearest 0.25 ms; either pauses), or press play to run 1 ms of string time per screen second; play stops at 20 ms and starts again from 0.
Measured
The string is d'Alembert's solution for zero initial velocity, sampled every 0.1 cm. u(0, t) is the displacement at the centre; max u, left and max u, right are the greatest displacement on x ≤ 0 and on x ≥ 0, all in mm.

The model
Infinite string released from rest · τ = 4.0 N, ρℓ = 0.010 kg/m, v = 20 m/s · small slopes, displacement drawn magnified · slowed: 1 ms takes 1 s · triangle and rectangle: formula taken as the limit of smooth pulses

Guided Inquiry

1 · Releasing the hump

Choose the smooth hump and set the time to 0. The string is held in a hump 2.00 mm high and is at rest. Before pressing play, predict what the released hump will do. Then press play and watch the string until t = 20 ms.

2 · The string at 10 ms

Keep the smooth hump and set the time to 0. The waves travel at v = 20 m/s. Before moving the time, predict what the string looks like at t = 10 ms. Then drag the time slider to 10 ms and read the axis and the readouts.

3 · Releasing a rectangle

Choose the rectangle, which puts the time back to 0. It is 2.00 mm high for |x| < 5.0 cm. Before moving the time, predict the shape of the string at t = 1.25 ms, when each part has moved vt = 2.5 cm. Then drag the time slider to 1.25 ms.

4 · The centre of the rectangle

Keep the rectangle and the time at 1.25 ms, where the centre reads u(0, t) = 2.00 mm. Before pressing play, predict how the displacement at the centre changes as the time runs on to 5 ms. Then press play and watch the readout u(0, t).

5 · Mapping the triangle

Choose the triangle, which puts the time back to 0 and clears the map. Before pressing play, predict the pattern the map of u over the x–t plane will show once the run has reached 20 ms. Then press play and watch the map fill in.

6 · Summary

A string released from rest splits into two half-height copies of its starting shape, u(x, t) = ½u0(x − vt) + ½u0(x + vt), which move apart at v = √(τ/ρℓ) = 20 m/s without changing shape. Where the copies overlap they add; on the x–t map each one travels along a straight line x ± vt = constant.

D'Alembert's Solution

01

At a glance

A taut string is held in a pulse and then let go from rest. This sim follows the string for 20 ms after the release, with a map that records its displacement over position and time.

What you'll learn

  • What a string released from rest does with its starting shape.
  • How the shape at a later time follows from the starting shape.
  • What the centre readout and the x–t map record.
The three starting shapes, each 2.0 mm high with half-width 5.0 cm.

What's on screen

  • The solid blue curve is the string u(x, t) over a dotted baseline, x from −50 to 50 cm and u from −0.5 to 2.5 mm. The vertical scale is magnified.
  • Dashed orange and purple curves join the string once a run has reached 20 ms.
  • The map below shows u over x and t, white at 0 and dark blue at 2.0 mm, with a thin line at the current time.

03

Two travelling waves solve the wave equation on an infinite string

A string with tension τ and mass per unit length ρℓ obeys the wave equation (notes 7.2), with v = √(τ/ρℓ). Here v = √(4.0/0.010) = 20 m/s.

With ξ = x − vt and η = x + vt, the equation becomes ∂²u/∂ξ∂η = 0, and on an infinite line its general solution is (7.7):

u(x, t) = f(x − vt) + g(x + vt)

where f and g are any twice-differentiable functions. The value of f(x − vt) at x and t is its value at x − vt at time zero, so the profile of f moves in the +x direction at speed v without changing its shape. In the same way g(x + vt) moves in the −x direction.

The initial displacement u0(x) and the initial velocity 𝒰(x) decide which f and g the string has. In the sim 𝒰 = 0.

Key idea. Whatever the starting shape, the later string is a right-moving wave plus a left-moving wave.
See itLook at the hump at 20 ms. Watch for: a dashed orange curve at x = +40 cm and a dashed purple one at x = −40 cm, with the string following both.
04

Released from rest, the pulse splits into two half-height copies

At t = 0, f + g = u0 and −vf′ + vg′ = 𝒰. Solving for f and g gives d'Alembert's solution (7.8):

u(x, t) = ½[u0(x − vt) + u0(x + vt)] + (1/2v) ∫x−vtx+vt 𝒰(x′) dx′

Released from rest means 𝒰 = 0, so the integral vanishes. Nothing favours either direction, and the pulse divides evenly: ½u0(x − vt) moves right and ½u0(x + vt) moves left.

Each copy has half the height of the released shape. At t = 0 the two copies lie on top of each other and add to u0, 2.00 mm at the peak, so each is 1.00 mm. Two full-height copies would add to 4.00 mm, which the string never had.

At 10 ms, vt = 20 m/s × 10 ms = 20 cm. The copies of the hump sit at x = ±20 cm, each 1.00 mm high, with exactly the shape of the released hump scaled down.

The notes' Fig. 60 for the sim's hump. Solid: the string. Dashed: the two copies, orange moving right, purple moving left.
See itLook at the hump at 10 ms. Watch for: two humps 1.00 mm high centred at x = ±20 cm, and max u reading 1.00 mm on each side.
05

Where the copies overlap they add, so a rectangle gives a step

At any time the string is the sum of the two copies. A rectangle shows this best, because its edges mark where each copy stands.

At t = 1.25 ms, vt = 2.5 cm. The right copy covers −2.5 to 7.5 cm and the left copy covers −7.5 to 2.5 cm, each 1.00 mm high. For |x| < 2.5 cm both are present, so the string reads 1.00 + 1.00 = 2.00 mm. From 2.5 cm out to 7.5 cm on each side only one copy is present, so it reads 1.00 mm.

The result is a stepped shape: 2.00 mm in the middle and 1.00 mm on the shoulders. Each copy still has its full width, 10 cm, and its own height, 1.00 mm. Only their positions have changed.

Rectangle at 1.25 ms. Dashed: the two 1.00 mm copies. Solid: their sum.
See itLook at the rectangle at 1.25 ms. Watch for: the 2.00 mm step for |x| < 2.5 cm and 1.00 mm shoulders out to 7.5 cm, with max u reading 2.00 mm.
06

The centre reads the released shape at x = vt

All three shapes are symmetric, u0(−x) = u0(x). At x = 0 the two copies are equal, so u(0, t) = u0(vt): the readout samples the released shape at the distance vt each copy has travelled from the centre. Here vt = 2 cm for every ms.

The rectangle is flat at 2.00 mm out to 5.0 cm, so u(0, t) stays 2.00 mm until the copies have moved vt = 5.0 cm, at 2.5 ms, and then drops to zero in one step. The triangle, u0(x) = 2.00 (1 − |x|/5.0 cm) mm, falls steadily: 1.00 mm at 1.25 ms and zero at 2.5 ms. The smooth hump, 2.00 e−(x/5.0 cm)² mm, has no edge. At 2.5 ms it reads 2.00 e−1 = 0.74 mm.

u(0, t) = u₀(vt) for the three shapes.
shape t

07

The x–t map shows two straight bands

Each copy depends on x − vt or x + vt only, so it is constant along the line x − vt = constant or x + vt = constant. On the map these are straight lines of slope fixed by v.

For the triangle, each band is 10 cm wide, the width of the triangle, and keeps one shade. At 20 ms their centres are at x = ±vt = ±40 cm. The bands are darker only near the bottom, where the two copies overlap. For the triangle that is while 2vt < 10 cm, that is for t < 2.5 ms.

Nothing here spreads out like heat: a function of x − vt keeps its width and its height, and only its position changes. Figure 60 of the notes is this picture for any pulse. Reflection at a fixed end (7.10) is the next use of the same f and g, and is not a control here.

The map for the triangle. Each copy travels along a straight line.
See itLook at the triangle at 20 ms. Watch for: two straight bands on the map meeting at the bottom, darker only there, with the copies at x = ±40 cm.
08

Summary

In one line. A string let go from rest in one of three starting shapes, followed for 20 ms, with the displacement at every position and time mapped.

Key points

  • u(x, t) = ½u0(x − vt) + ½u0(x + vt), with v = √(τ/ρℓ) = 20 m/s.
  • Two copies, each half the height and the same width, move apart and add where they overlap.
  • The centre reads u0(vt). On the map each copy is a straight band.

Common mix-ups

  • "The whole hump moves off to the right, still 2.00 mm high." Released from rest, half goes each way, 1.00 mm high.
  • "The hump just sinks and nothing travels." Nothing damps this string, so both copies run out at v.
  • "Each copy keeps the full height." At t = 0 they add to u0, so each is ½u0.
  • "The copies spread and fall, like heat." A function of x − vt keeps its shape: max u stays 1.00 mm.

Things to try on your own

  • Predict the triangle's centre at 1.25 ms, then read it.
  • Find when the rectangle's two copies stop overlapping.
